Generate a large sample and inspect length, uniqueness, randomness, and URL-safe encoding. Pass: at least 128 independent random bits and no predictable sequence.

Pass: success consumes once and cannot be reopened.

Pre-hijacking. An attacker signs up with the victim's email and picks the password. The victim later gets a confirmation email (or signs in with Google), and the account becomes legitimately confirmed, with the attacker's password still on it. The design stops direct PKCE confirmation, but it doesn't address a real owner confirming an account whose password they never set. Fix: make the confirmation step set the password, or discard any pre-confirmation password and revoke sessions at confirmation.

Signup metadata. The public signup call accepts a free-form data object that becomes user_metadata. If any trigger, RPC or onboarding screen reads role, age, guardian status or school from there, a teen can sign up as an adult poster by calling Supabase directly. The spec says the hook assigns no roles, but it never says the existing triggers ignore metadata. Audit every reader of raw_user_meta_data.

Attacker text in your own email. A display name or other signup field that lands in the greeting turns your legitimate auth@mortapp.org message into a phishing vehicle. Don't put any user-supplied field in the email, and ignore redirect_to and similar fields in the hook payload even though they arrive in it.

Link swap. The attacker requests a valid link for their own account and sends it to a victim. The victim "resets their password" on the attacker's account and then enters personal info or payment details into it. Fix: show the masked address on every confirm and reset screen.

Notification previews. If the 8-digit code is in the subject line or first line, anyone who glances at a teen's lock screen can read it. Keep the code out of the subject, and consider making the link primary.

Timing oracle from the hook. GoTrue waits for the Send Email hook. A recovery request for an existing account then takes as long as the SMTP send, while an unknown address returns immediately. That is an account-existence oracle in plain response time. Fix: queue the send and return from the hook quickly, or pad responses.

Email-parser mismatch. Addresses with quoted local parts, extra @ symbols, or non-ASCII characters can be read one way by the provider's validator and another way by your SMTP library. The challenge is then bound to one address but delivered to a different one. Fix: assert that the SMTP envelope recipient exactly equals the bound address, and reject exotic syntax.

Lowercase differences. Go, Deno and Postgres don't always lowercase identically (locale-sensitive cases like the Turkish dotless i). A registry key built in one runtime can then fail to match, or wrongly match, in another. Use one canonicalization point and test across all three.

IPv6 rotation. One home connection controls a /64, which is 2^64 addresses. Any per-IP limit, including the "independent abuse limit" for unknown identifiers, is useless unless it aggregates by prefix.

Killing someone else's code. A resend invalidates the previous challenge, and resend requests are unauthenticated. An attacker can request a resend for a victim every cooldown period, so the victim's code dies before they finish typing. Consider keeping the previous challenge valid until a new one is delivered, or until a short grace period passes.

Mail-bombing and sender reputation. Free signups against victim addresses flood their inboxes. The resulting spam complaints can get auth@mortapp.org or the whole domain flagged, and then real users stop receiving codes. Add per-recipient and global send ceilings, and monitor complaint rates.

Hot-row lock contention. Hammering one challenge ID makes everyone queue on its row lock, including the legitimate user. Short-circuit exhausted or unknown IDs before taking the lock, and set lock_timeout.

Same-origin exposure. The auth page lives on mortapp.org, the same origin as a marketplace with user-generated content, and the Next.js shell may load analytics or cinematic WebGL scripts. One XSS in a job post, or one third-party script, can read the secret or password in memory. Fix: host auth on its own origin or subdomain with its own CSP, with nothing else loaded.

Mail gateways and fragments. Some security gateways and clients rewrite links or drop #fragments. Developers then "fix" this by moving the secret into the query string, which puts it in logs. Test the major mail clients before activation.

Android link interception. If the link can open the Flutter app through an unverified deep link, another installed app can claim it. Use verified App Links (assetlinks.json) and keep the browser as the default.

Console and admin routes. Dashboard buttons ("confirm user", "send recovery") and the Admin generate_link route mint credentials outside your checker. List every such route in the guard's allowlist test.

Recycled addresses. Expired school or personal domains get re-registered, and the new owner receives mail for old addresses. Email proof can't fix this, so consider notifying the old address on recovery and requiring step-up for sensitive actions.

Forge Host, forwarded host, origin, and destination headers. Pass: no trusted recipient, redirect, policy, or tenant is selected from untrusted headers.
Compare error text, response size, headers, and timing across known/unknown account, challenge, purpose, and delivery states. Pass: no useful enumeration oracle.
Submit invalid password input with a valid recovery capability. Pass: validation fails before capability consumption or Admin dispatch, according to the documented policy.
Attempt recovery on an unconfirmed account. Pass: it cannot implicitly confirm the account or create private proof; only the specified owner-controlled transition is allowed.
Delay an authorized provider mutation and issue repeated writes. Pass: pending markers and operation leases prevent replay, duplicate writes, and premature success display.

Trigger credential updates through every supported provider path that can run during the operation. Pass: the mutation guard validates live account/address/grant state inside the provider transaction.

Restore a database snapshot containing pre-restore terminal states. Pass: redemption is disabled until pre-restore challenge/capability/operation generations are retired or invalidated by trusted post-restore state.

Roll back hooks and browser components as one coherent state transition. Pass: the system records which guarantees remain, does not reopen consumed items, and does not claim the new five-attempt guarantee after restoring the old flow.

Before destructive tests, assert project/containers are `mort-mobile`, Auth is the expected loopback endpoint, and the database is the matching local database. Pass: hosted endpoints, Loop containers, real SMTP hosts, and other projects abort.

Run rotating-caller tests only with synthetic local caller contexts and bounded concurrency, request/time limits, cleanup, and an abort threshold. Pass: no public proxies, external traffic, global Docker reconfiguration, or emulator is used.
Run version-drift tests in a separate local fixture. Pass: the working stack is not upgraded or mutated as a side effect.
Use fake local SMTP credentials for fault/TLS/header tests. Pass: no real SMTP stress mail is sent; SPF/DKIM/DMARC checks remain separately authorized delivery tests.

Treat service-role compromise as a threat-model boundary while still auditing client-secret exposure and rotating only disposable local fixture credentials. Pass: no public bypass is justified by service-role assumptions.

Record source ID, redacted request shape, caller role, fixture version, timing/concurrency, expected/observed result, permitted counter changes, state digest, sanitized-log check, and cleanup. Pass: failed or incomplete cleanup cases remain `NOT_RUN`/failed, and overlapping documents are mapped to stable IDs rather than counted as independent passing tests.
